doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Escaping Cuba in the Mariel boatlift
summary: Peruvian Embassy crisis led Castro to open the port; Berroa escaped at 26 and arrived in May 1980.

blocks.x: So when this opportunity came, if I understand the boatlift, there is a short window where Castro allowed quite a number of people to leave. How did you qualify for that? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

I didn’t qualify. I escaped. Meaning, there was so much confusion. That was an event that surprised Castro, it really did. And the events, the Mariel events were happening because for at the Peruvian Embassy in Havana. A group of people took a bus and they slammed the bus into the Peruvian Embassy. All the embassies in Cuba that granted, let’s say, an embassy from capitalist countries, all of them had guards. Guards. People waiting in line. You wouldn’t have allowed to not even walk at embassy. I remember I was dating a lady that at the end became my wife in Cuba and she used to live two blocks away from the Argentinean consulate or embassy. And I used to pick her up and we were started going down the street and you know we were young and so we were like talking and kissing and holding hands, not realizing that we were about to walk through this street where the embassy was at. And we were coming and talking and the next thing we will hear was a whistle and saw the guard signaling us to go to the sidewalk. You weren’t even allowed to walk through the middle of the street. In the middle of the street that was a no walking zone. So every embassy had guards. So this guy’s bus at the Peruvian Embassy they had an exchange of crossfire because the Cuban government claimed that those guys had gone. That was never proven. There was a crossfire and one of the guards was killed, got killed. Castro asked the Peruvian Embassy to surrender, to give those people back to him and the Peruvian ambassador told him this guy has asked for political asylum and my country grants belief in political asylum, and then I’m going to give the guy back to you. Those guys are going to Peru. And then he said, “Well I’m not going to allow them to go to Peru.” He got into a feud with the ambassador and then he got mad. He was a very [gap] guy and he said, “Well if you don’t give me the guys I’m going to take the guards off your embassy.” And the ambassador said, “We need no guards. It is you that have guards in our embassy to prevent people coming here to ask for political asylum. He took the guards off and in less than 24 hours, Monk, 10,000 people walked into the house. The embassy was like a huge house, like one of those houses in Connecticut or Upstate New York you know, upper class people. That was the embassy. Now can you imagine 10,000 people in your front yard or around your houses jumping the fences and then in 24 hours you have 10,000 people. So they had to close the streets and so forth and so on. He got mad, and that’s when he said, “It seems like there are a group of people in this country that don’t want to be here. They don’t like the revolution, so I’m going to rehabilitate this port for everyone. He said that very clear. Everyone who wanted to leave the island, do so. So immediately families here in Miami started taking and renting boats and going to Cuba to get their families. That’s how, in that confusion, I was in serious political trouble in Cuba for being a big mouth, and I called my family in New York. I have family in New York and one of my family went down to Cuba to pick me up. So among that confusion, because then Castro realized that professionals were leaving the island, © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

doctors, engineers and so on and so forth. So in order for him to take the attention away from that he started sending prisoners, people that were suffering from dementia, he started to make it look like every Cuban that wanted to leave the island was a low class person.
But anyway in that confusion I escaped. I left. They didn’t realize who I was and I was lucky. I was super lucky. And I left the island.
And you were about 17? Is that right?
I was 26 when I left Cuba. I was 26. I arrived here in May 1980 and I turned 27 July 1980. I was 26 years old.
